candidate.title: Context-aware adaptive computing under resource constraints
candidate.workingTitle: Context-Aware Adaptive Computing Under Resource Constraints
candidate.summary: How can a context-aware computing system adapt service behaviour to constrained or changing networks and devices while preserving task completion and acceptable quality?
candidate.shortDescription: An exploratory systems-research direction grounded in context-aware, adaptive computing infrastructure under constrained conditions.
candidate.ghanaianRelevance: Constrained connectivity and power are a plausible setting. They do not define the system under study.
candidate.technicalContribution: A bounded, context-aware adaptation policy for one selected application/system class. Candidate control levers include content quality, synchronisation frequency, offline-first behaviour, local processing, data transmission, and task prioritisation. The contribution must be a policy plus reproducible comparison, not simply a prototype.

feasibility.rationale: This is a planning assessment. The direction is technically workable only after the system class, decision, and metrics are chosen.

candidate.dataRequirements: One selected application/system, reproducible workloads, and network/device profiles reflecting constrained bandwidth, latency, intermittent connectivity, battery/energy, CPU, and memory. Use measured traces or controlled emulation; do not claim the profiles represent all Ghanaian users without evidence.
candidate.evaluationDesign: Compare a static baseline with an adaptive policy across stable and constrained profiles. Measure data consumption, latency, energy, task completion, synchronisation reliability, CPU/memory use, and service/output quality. Define user-relevant acceptable quality and task-completion criteria before testing.
majorRisks: The current idea is an area, not a bounded research problem, until the system class and adaptation decision are selected.
The work could become a generic prototype without a testable policy or clear baseline.
No candidate-specific literature map or dataset/workload selection has yet been completed.
openDecisions: Which application or computing system provides a bounded, testable use case?
Which adaptation levers are controllable and which are out of scope?
What context signals trigger each adaptation?
What service-quality and task-completion thresholds define acceptable behaviour?
Which network/device profiles and workload traces can be reproduced?

nodes.title: Static behaviour under changing resources
nodes.summary: Systems that keep one execution strategy can fail when bandwidth, power, or connectivity changes.
nodes.detail: The broader research orientation discussed in the project includes human-centred intelligent systems and human-centred computing infrastructure: IT should be context-relevant, adaptive, and useful rather than becoming a “white elephant.” A possible systems problem is that computing services operate under changing bandwidth, connectivity, energy, memory, and processing limits, while static execution strategies may not respond. This remains a framing hypothesis until one system and adaptation decision are chosen. Specific adaptation levers discussed include reducing content quality, changing synchronisation frequency, prioritising tasks, using offline-first behaviour, shifting work to local processing, and controlling data transmission.
assumptions: A measurable system can be isolated and exercised under controlled resource profiles.
The resource constraints can be modelled without making unsupported claims about all Ghanaian infrastructure.
risks: The topic stays an area survey unless one system and one decision are chosen.

nodes.title: How should a bounded computing system adapt to changing resource availability while maintaining acceptable service quality?
nodes.summary: How can a system adapt resource use or service behaviour and still hold an acceptable level of performance or quality?
nodes.detail: The question must be operationalised by selecting one system class, one adaptation decision, a workload, measurable resource variables, and a service-quality threshold. Without those choices, the topic remains too broad to test. Candidate measurements discussed include data use, latency, energy, task completion, synchronisation reliability, CPU, and memory. The final metric set depends on the selected application and adaptation levers.

nodes.title: A systems question, once it is bounded
nodes.summary: The contribution would be a policy and a comparison, not a user interface.
nodes.detail: This direction aligns with the project’s accepted research orientation: both human-centred intelligent systems and human-centred computing infrastructure. The system should adapt to actual context and constraints, rather than assume ideal connectivity, power, or hardware. The Ghanaian context motivates realistic resource profiles; the thesis contribution remains a computing-systems method.

nodes.title: Infrastructure constraints are a possible setting
nodes.summary: Infrastructure constraints are a possible setting
nodes.detail: Unreliable connectivity and limited power are relevant in many Ghanaian deployments. That setting does not choose the system for the thesis.

nodes.summary: An adaptation policy with a measured trade-off
nodes.detail: The technical core should be a defined adaptation mechanism/policy and its measured behaviour under resource variation. The work should include a static baseline, controlled workloads, repeatable resource profiles, and explicit trade-off analysis.

nodes.title: Choosing the system that adapts
nodes.summary: Choosing the system that adapts
nodes.detail: Edge, fog, or mobile computing are areas, not yet a thesis problem. One system class has to be chosen. Candidate contexts include mobile or edge applications operating under constrained connectivity, limited battery, and variable device capacity. The application must be selected before the topic is considered bounded.

nodes.detail: No candidate-specific literature review has been completed in the project discussions. Edge, fog, and mobile computing were considered possible system classes, but none has been selected. Do not present generic adaptive-computing statements as literature findings.

nodes.title: A single-resource objective may ignore the rest of the trade-off
nodes.summary: A single-resource objective may ignore the rest of the trade-off
nodes.detail: A possible concern is that an adaptation policy may optimise one resource while under-reporting other resource costs or service quality. This is a proposed evaluation concern, not a confirmed literature gap. It must be tested against a focused set of studies after the system class is chosen.

nodes.title: Static versus adaptive policies
nodes.summary: Static versus adaptive policies
nodes.detail: The comparison that would make the work empirical: a fixed policy against a policy that reacts. The adaptive policy could change quality, synchronisation, offline/local processing, data transmission, or task priority in response to network/device context. Only a small, coherent subset should be selected.

nodes.title: Static policies are the obvious baseline
nodes.summary: Static policies are the obvious baseline
nodes.detail: A fixed/static policy is the natural baseline for testing whether adaptation helps under changing resource availability. The project has not yet selected a workload, trace, or resource profile, so this is an experimental-design requirement rather than a finding about prior literature.

nodes.title: Adaptive policies may be tested on workloads that do not change
nodes.summary: Adaptive policies may be tested on workloads that do not change
nodes.detail: A candidate question is whether policies evaluated on narrow or static workloads remain effective when resource availability changes. No studies have been reviewed for this candidate, so this is a hypothesis to investigate, not an established gap.

nodes.title: The objective is unspecified
nodes.summary: The objective is unspecified
nodes.detail: The discussions identified latency, energy, memory, bandwidth, and output/service quality as distinct dimensions. Optimising one alone does not establish that the system remains useful to its user or workload. Candidate user-centred outcomes include successful task completion and synchronisation reliability, alongside system metrics such as data consumption, latency, energy, CPU, and memory.

nodes.title: Joint reporting of resource use and service quality is easy to omit
nodes.summary: Joint reporting of resource use and service quality is easy to omit
nodes.detail: A candidate methodological contribution is joint reporting of resource consumption and service quality, including an explicit threshold for acceptable output or service. This is currently a design requirement; literature support has not yet been established. The relevant comparison should report the trade-off between resource savings and task/service quality. A policy that saves bandwidth or energy by making the application unusable is not a successful adaptation.
